title: Self-Leveling Compound Calculator
description: Work out 50 lb bags of self-leveling compound from floor area and average depth, with maker coverage charts and an example.

cover.alt: Self-leveling compound poured from a bucket and spread with a gauge rake

keywords: how many bags of self leveler
takeaways: Bags = floor area in sq ft divided by the sq ft per bag at your pour depth, from the maker chart.
A 50 lb bag covers about 48 to 50 sq ft at 1/8 in deep, and only about 24 to 25 sq ft at 1/4 in deep.
Average depth, not the deepest spot, drives the bag count, so measure the floor on a grid.
body:
A 50 lb bag of self-leveling compound covers about 48 to 50 sq ft at 1/8 in (3 mm) deep, and coverage halves each time depth doubles. A 240 sq ft room at an average 1/4 in needs 10 bags before a spare, and 11 in the cart. This guide shows the maker charts and the math.

## The formula and the coverage charts

**Bags = area in sq ft / coverage in sq ft per bag at your average depth.**

Average depth is the key input. It is not the deepest hole and not the high spot. The method below shows how to find it.

Mapei lists this coverage for a 50 lb bag of Self-Leveler Plus.

| Average depth | Coverage per 50 lb bag |
| --- | --- |
| 1/8 in (3 mm) | 48 sq ft |
| 1/4 in (6 mm) | 24 sq ft |
| 1/2 in (12 mm) | 12 sq ft |
| 1 in (25 mm) | 6 sq ft |

Custom Building Products lists near identical figures for LevelQuik: 50 sq ft at 1/8 in, 25 at 1/4 in, 12.5 at 1/2 in, and 6.25 at 1 in per 50 lb bag. TEC lists 48 to 54 sq ft at 1/8 in for its 50 lb EZ Level product. Three makers land in the same band, so plan on the low figure, 48 sq ft at 1/8 in.

Double the depth, halve the coverage. That check lets you spot a bad quote fast. If a bid lists 5 bags for 240 sq ft at 1/4 in, the math is wrong, because 240 / 24 is 10 bags before any spare.

Plan the finish floor too. Our [flooring calculator](/blog/flooring-calculator/) gives boxes of plank to go over the leveled floor, and our [tile calculator](/blog/tile-calculator/) gives tile counts if the room will be tiled.

## Worked example: a 240 sq ft room at 1/4 in average depth

Your room is 12 x 20 ft (3.7 x 6.1 m), so the floor is 240 sq ft. A grid check shows the low side needs about 3/8 in and the high side needs about 1/8 in, for an average pour depth of 1/4 in over the whole room. You will prime first, then pour.

Step 1: Area = 12 x 20 = 240 sq ft.

Step 2: Coverage at 1/4 in on the Mapei chart = 24 sq ft per 50 lb bag.

Step 3: Bags = 240 / 24 = 10 bags.

Step 4: Add one spare bag for spillage and bucket loss. Buy 11 bags, plus primer.

Check the math a second way by volume. Volume = 240 sq ft x 0.25 in / 12 = 5.0 cu ft of compound. One bag at 1/8 in covers 48 sq ft, which is 48 x 0.125 / 12 = 0.5 cu ft per bag. Bags = 5.0 / 0.5 = 10 bags. Both methods agree, then add the same spare bag for 11 total.

Water matters too. Each bag takes a set amount from the data sheet, about 5 to 5.3 quarts for the Mapei product. Too much water weakens the pour. Measure water in a marked bucket for every mix.

## How to find your average depth

Set a grid of screws or use a laser level and a tape. On a screw grid, drill small holes a few feet apart, set screws, and raise them to one level plane at least 1/8 in over the highest point. The gap from floor to each screw head is the depth at that point. Add the gaps and divide by the number of points. That average goes in the formula.

Fine Homebuilding describes this screw grid method, with the plane set about 1/8 in over the high point. It takes 20 minutes and saves the most common error in this job, guessing depth from the worst corner.

Mark the depth on the wall with tape as a pour guide. Seal the edges before you mix anything. This compound runs like thin pancake batter. It will find a drain, a pipe gap, and a crack to the room below. Foam backer rod, tape, and a board across each doorway keep it in the room. Prime the full floor first. Unprimed concrete and wood pull water from the mix and can break the bond.

## What changes the bag count

A wavy floor uses more than a flat slope at the same average. Peaks get the minimum cover and valleys get filled, so the true average sits higher than a two-point check suggests. On a rough floor, add 10 to 15 percent to the bag count instead of one spare bag.

Old adhesive and paint change bond, not volume, but they add prep and primer coats. Scrape and clean first. Some products allow a pour up to 1 in or 1.5 in in one lift. Past that, the maker may call for a second lift or added aggregate. Deep fills get costly fast. A thick low area can be cheaper to fill with a cement patch first, then a thin leveler skin. Compare with our [underlayment calculator](/blog/underlayment-calculator/) guide if the floor needs build-up for laminate or vinyl.

Room shape changes waste. Long halls and L-shaped rooms spill more mix at the edges than one open rectangle. Buy the spare bag. A pour cannot pause while someone drives to the store. The mix has a flow time of about 10 to 15 minutes for the Mapei product, so the full count must be on site before the first bucket is mixed.

## Mistakes that ruin a pour

The first mistake is no primer. The second is no edge seal, and the compound escapes under a wall. Both are cheap to prevent and hard to fix.

The third mistake is one person mixing and pouring a big room alone. The flow window is short. A two-person team is the normal setup for rooms over about 150 sq ft. Have water measured and tools in reach before you start.

The fourth mistake is laying flooring too early. Mapei lists tile work at about 24 hours after a pour up to 1/4 in, and 2 to 3 days for other coverings at 1/4 to 1/2 in. A soft pour under hard tile can crack the tile.

Call a pro if the floor has moving cracks, a flexing wood subfloor, or a slope that points to a framing problem. Leveler hides shape. It does not fix structure.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many bags of self-leveler do I need for 100 sq ft?
At 1/8 in average depth, 100 / 48 = 2.08 bags, rounded up to 3 bags with a spare in mind, or 2 bags plus risk. At 1/4 in, 100 / 24 = 4.17 bags, rounded up to 5 bags. Depth doubles the count.

### How much does one 50 lb bag cover?
Maker charts list about 48 to 50 sq ft at 1/8 in, 24 to 25 sq ft at 1/4 in, and 12 to 12.5 sq ft at 1/2 in per 50 lb bag. Use the chart on your exact product, because the range is small but real.

### Can I pour self-leveler over plywood?
Some products allow it over exterior grade plywood with primer and, in some systems, lath. Others are concrete only. The data sheet decides. A flexing wood floor will crack a rigid pour, so fix bounce first or choose a different floor prep.

### How thick can I pour in one go?
Mapei Self-Leveler Plus lists a single lift range of 1/8 in to 1 in, with a minimum of 1/8 in over the highest point. Custom LevelQuik lists up to 1.5 in in one pour. Past the listed range, plan a second lift or a patch fill first.

### Do I need primer under self-leveler?
Yes, on the systems in the charts above. Primer seals the substrate, helps bond, and stops pinholes from air rising out of concrete. Skipping primer is the most common cause of a pour that peels or bubbles.

## Next step
